## Summary

Eisman argues that mortgage lock-in, constrained local supply and rising ownership costs explain housing’s weakness despite better-run builders. He distinguishes builders from companies exposed to existing-home transactions and favors supply reforms over buyer subsidies. FHFA loan-level research supports the lock-in mechanism; other quantitative and causal claims need matched evidence. He also discusses AI risks to software franchises, skepticism about crypto valuation and ETF structure. His practical fund comparison is mostly sound, but passive portfolios do change with their indices and not every mutual fund is actively managed.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

<a id="CEzkZcvZ0rU-c013"></a>
### 013. Many owners retain much cheaper mortgages than current market rates, discouraging moves and restricting existing-home supply.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 9:24-10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CEzkZcvZ0rU&t=564s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

FHFA’s primary loan-level study measures lower sale probability when market rates exceed existing rates and upward price pressure from the supply restriction. This supports the mechanism, not every cited December 2025 quantity.

Assessment test: Update the loan-level rate gap and sale-probability estimates.

- [The Lock-In Effect of Rising Mortgage Rates, Working Paper 24-03](https://www.fhfa.gov/research/papers/wp2403) (2024-03-18): Primary loan-level research estimates higher market rates relative to existing loans reduce sale probability. Original abstract estimates 1.33 million prevented sales in 2022Q2-2023Q4 and upward price pressure from reduced supply. Estimates support the mechanism, not every December 2025 market statistic.

### 018. On a fully financed $400,000 thirty-year mortgage, moving from four to 6.25 percent raises principal-and-interest payments from about $1,900 to $2,500.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 13:08-13:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CEzkZcvZ0rU&t=788s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Using payment=P*r/(1-(1+r)^(-360)) gives approximately $1,910 and $2,463 at monthly rates 0.04/12 and 0.0625/12. Rounded illustrative payments are reasonable; taxes, insurance and down payment are excluded.

Conditional reasoning: Using payment=P*r/(1-(1+r)^(-360)) gives approximately $1,910 and $2,463 at monthly rates 0.04/12 and 0.0625/12. Rounded illustrative payments are reasonable; taxes, insurance and down payment are excluded.

Assessment test: Recalculate standard fixed-rate amortization for the stated assumptions.

<a id="CEzkZcvZ0rU-c027"></a>
### 027. Passive ETFs track a specified index at generally low fees, while active funds pay managers to select securities.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 17:44-18:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CEzkZcvZ0rU&t=1064s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

SEC confirms index-tracking and active ETF strategies. The accompanying claim that passive portfolios never change is too absolute: tracking a changing index requires portfolio changes. Mutual funds can also be passive.

Assessment test: Inspect the relevant index methodology and fund prospectus rather than treating legal structure as strategy.

- [Updated investor bulletin on exchange-traded funds](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-24) (2023-02-23): Retail ETF shares trade in secondary markets. Authorized participants create/redeem large units, typically with in-kind baskets. ETF selling therefore need not mechanically cause an equivalent cash sale by the fund; index and ETF flow effects require separate analysis.

## Framework and tools

- Separate new-home and existing-home transaction exposure.
- Compare earnings deterioration with stock expectations before assuming fundamentals are improving.
- Model mortgage payments explicitly and distinguish liquidity lock-in from construction constraints.
- Compare demand subsidies with supply elasticity.
- Evaluate fund structure, costs and taxes separately from manager skill.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Builder and building-product company EPS and share-return tables
- Zelman entry-level affordability index including taxes and insurance
- Illustrative $400,000 thirty-year mortgage at 4% and 6.25%
- Mortgage rate distribution, public builder market share and housing shortage estimates
- ETF fees, trading, disclosure and in-kind redemption

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
- He corrects an earlier electricity-unit error from terawatts to terawatt-hours.
- The mortgage example assumes full financing and excludes taxes and insurance.
- Historical and current fund terminology is simplified; mutual fund is a legal structure, not a synonym for active management.
